title: How Fire Breathing Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore fire breathing as part of the circus and fire arts. They cover the history (ancient Persia and naphtha, 19th-century circuses, Gene Simmons of KISS popularizing it in the 1970s through a tribute-band guy), why it is extremely dangerous, the mist-and-angle technique (60 to 80 degrees), site recon for wind and power lines, fuel choices (avoiding gasoline and alcohol, kerosene/paraffin, lamp oil, Coleman fuel, corn starch), blowback, torches, fire eater pneumonia, long-term health effects, safety crews and fire marshals, and fire eating, poi, and fire breathing world records. The episode ends with a message break, a Coed (Cooperative for Education) scholarship announcement, and a listener mail story about An American Werewolf in London.

segments.title: Opening banter and circus arts
segments.summary: The hosts joke about past circus-themed episodes and the film The Place Beyond the Pines, then introduce fire breathing as the next circus art and discuss the name 'fire aspirating'.

segments.title: History of fire breathing
segments.summary: Fire breathing's possible origins in ancient Persia and naphtha, its rise with 19th-century circuses, and its 1970s revival attributed to Gene Simmons of KISS, who taught a Black Diamond tribute-band member.

segments.title: Why fire breathing is dangerous
segments.summary: Fire arts are introduced, with fire breathing described as the most dangerous. Professionals typically won't teach it through podcasts or websites, and learning requires an experienced teacher.

segments.title: Technique: mist, angle, and breath
segments.summary: Fire breathing needs fuel, a flame, and a mouth. The fuel must be atomized into a mist with spit, held at a 60 to 80 degree angle, and performed with controlled exhalation. Beginners train with water for a long time.

segments.title: Site preparation and fuel choice
segments.summary: Performers check wind, power lines, bystanders, and nearby trees first. They avoid gasoline and alcohol because of toxicity and low flash points, which cause blowback. Kerosene, paraffin, lamp oil, Coleman fuel, and corn starch are discussed with their trade-offs.

segments.title: Torches, health risks, and safety crews
segments.summary: Torch construction and material hazards are covered. Health risks include fire eater pneumonia (hydrocarbon pneumonitis) and long-term effects. Professionals use safety assistants, first aid kits, and coordinate with fire marshals.

segments.title: Fire eating, poi, and world records
segments.summary: Fire eating is covered, including extinguishing a torch in the mouth and lighting cigars from a held fume. Poi are introduced as flaming props. Several fire breathing world records are listed.

segments.title: Coed scholarship announcement and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts announce that Coed reached its scholarship goal, thank donors, and read a listener story about watching An American Werewolf in London as an eight year old and a neighbor's mental health episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts remind listeners of the danger and ask for listener stories, giving social and email contact information.
